title: Why Is One More Day in Stardew Valley Never Enough?

research.citation: Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng (2006), The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention, Journal of Marketing Research 43(1), 39–58
research.claim: In a café loyalty programme, customers purchased coffee more frequently as they neared a free-coffee reward. Additional field/online studies supported a goal-gradient pattern. This did not test Stardew Valley or game engagement.

research.citation: Nunes & Drèze (2006), The Endowed Progress Effect: How Artificial Advancement Increases Effort, Journal of Consumer Research 32(4), 504–512
research.claim: In reward-programme field experiments, giving customers apparent initial progress (two pre-stamped spaces on a ten-stamp card) increased completion relative to an unstamped eight-stamp card, although both required eight further purchases. The result concerns loyalty programmes, not in-game farm goals.

description: A 100-second research-informed lesson on why near-complete goals may make Stardew Valley's day-to-day tasks compelling. Demonstrates goal-gradient findings with coffee and car-wash reward programmes, then explicitly labels the application to crops and construction as an untested game-design interpretation. Visuals must show genuine HD Stardew Valley farming gameplay from the catalogued source; no static images or fabricated scenes. Review only, never auto-publish.

youtube_description:
Why does one more day in Stardew Valley so often become three? We explain the goal-gradient effect using actual reward-programme research, then explore a cautious interpretation of Stardew Valley's nearly complete goals.

Primary research:
Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng (2006): https://doi.org/10.1509/jmkr.43.1.39
Nunes & Drèze (2006): https://doi.org/10.1086/500480

These experiments studied loyalty programmes, not Stardew Valley players. The game-design application is an inference, not a demonstrated causal effect.
